en: Preface to the Sublime Truth from the West:
It is heard that the sixteen characters of the Court of Yu elaborated upon the transmission of the mind-dharma and the governance of the state;

the five thousand words of the Most High expounded the principles of the Way, its Virtue, and the divine immortals. Examining the Buddhist scriptures of our own tradition, one finds they all embody the true exposition.

Tracing back to the single source of the Three Teachings, it is only the Sūtras that remain unchanging and enable all sentient beings to ascend to the shore of enlightenment. In the Buddha’s words, there is compassion;
thus, the numinous roots of the Pure Land possess unimpeded eloquence. Regarding the secret scriptures of the Brahma Palace, the legacy of wisdom has been heard in its subtle traces.
By means of this, they serve as a ladder for broad salvation and deliverance—how could their purpose be limited merely to forming karmic ties through incense and lamps? Now, the Master Hanxu...
Xuánxià was a disciple who concurrently cultivated the power of precepts and meditative concentration.
He gave rise to the intention to edit and disseminate [the teachings], hoping to exhort his fellow disciples and taking their proclamation as his daily practice.

He thus selected what was secretly preserved in the oral transmission on palm leaves and that which was upheld by the *upāsikā* Sai, compiling them into a book to ensure its longevity throughout the world. Tracing the branches back to the source, he provided support...

As for its initial publication: the various chapters and dharanis of such works as the *Gao Wang Guan Shi Yin Jing*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, and others were compiled into a single volume and presented to the Imperial Preceptor Lü, the Muni Buddha.
Having read and certified them as excellent, he commanded that the sublime truths brought from the West be used to inscribe the title upon the cover.
Alas! The teaching of the Śākya clan has long been obscured. Among its seven consciousnesses, delusions abound; among its four bonds, one is easily ensnared.
While others merely resent the sharp wit of the "chisel-handle" [koan], who will deliver the staff and shout that strikes at the very head?

Yet you alone have fanned the light of the fire-stick and cleared away the gravel of the sands of saṃsāra, intending to open the gate of purity so that others may enter the realm of Vairocana. This vow is indeed worthy of praise.

How magnificent! Yet consider those who say: "The great canon in its lapis lazuli cases fills the rafters with its remaining volumes; the jade statutes of the Dharma-gate transmit the lamp of wondrous intent.
Awakening and entry are beyond words, and the realization of cause and effect is achieved through the clear mirror of Bodhi. All things ultimately return to formlessness;

why then must one wait for the morning bells and evening drums before being exhorted to diligent cultivation? They fail to realize that the benefit of written words lies precisely in their ability to open the seal of the Truth.

The diligence of recitation and study serves to dispel the obstacles of desire; though this [text] may be divided like the *tí* rice among the grain, it is truly sufficient to encompass the Three Vehicles.
If one sincerely applies oneself to its investigation and refinement, how would it differ from the transmission of the staff and robe?

It shall cause the field of the emotions to yield its own harvest and the ocean of nature to be free of dust, with the *svastika* (*wanzi*) emblazoned upon the breast as one takes refuge in the Golden Heaven. After three years of facing the wall, when the time comes for the plum fruits to ripen, the great assembly shall arrive.

A single laugh at the plucking of the flower. Layman, have you smelled the fragrance of the osmanthus? If you truly recognize that mind is itself Buddha, what need is there to debate whether formlessness is not emptiness?
Thus, it is not merely a matter of upholding and propagating the patriarchal style; rather, one’s faith has already opened to the nectar of immortality.
It is as if the Great Awakened One had entered a mountain of jewels, yet his hands remained empty. "Thus have I heard": may this light cause even the heads of stubborn stones to be enlightened.
In the summer of the year Wuyin (1638), Xue Qiu respectfully wrote this preface at the Taisheng Room of the Liaohua Immortal Pavilion in Wulin.
Subsequent Postscript.

Now, among the scriptures and dhāraṇīs transmitted through the ages, the *Gao Wang Guanshiyin Jing*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī*, and the *Cundi Dhāraṇī* have been most enduring.
Those who faithfully believe in, uphold, and recite them are numerous, and those who thereby eliminate transgressions and obtain blessings are infinite.
Thus, as for the spiritual manifestations and actual records documented in various sūtras and mantra texts, one cannot know how many there are.

Although some have been published—whether as sūtra manuscripts or mantra diagrams—they have not yet been compiled into a single collection; consequently, while they are easy to print and distribute, they remain incomplete and lacking in a unified compilation.

Having long revered the study of the profound mysteries (xuanxue) yet remaining unacquainted with the practice of dhyāna, I was first graced by the Great Being’s selection and recording of these works.
The lineage of supreme wisdom was transmitted;
furthermore, he received the Buddha’s grace and was granted a prediction of enlightenment.

Having attained realization and been bestowed with a name, he has been nurtured by the cultivation of the Sage’s virtue. Yet, looking back upon his own meager efforts, he finds himself unable to repay it. Thus, from among the Chan materials compiled within the *Tongshan lu* (Record of Universal Goodness)...

I have extracted the essential scriptures, mantras, and periods for fasting to benefit the world, so that those who revere them may hold these texts morning and evening without being burdened by a proliferation of scrolls.
As for the factual accounts of their spiritual efficacy, they are all contained within the respective sections of the *Tongshan lu* (Record of Shared Goodness) and need not be listed here;

this is intended to ensure clarity and brevity. Furthermore, I have commissioned my friend Shi You, whose courtesy name is Tongxuanle, to transcribe these characters with reverence for publication. The printing blocks are stored at Xī... [location].
Printed and circulated at the Huizhong Jingfang (Wisdom Emptiness Scripture Hall) of Lake Zhaoqing, in order to propagate its transmission.
Written with reverence by Wujing Zhou Shangzhi in the Wuyin year of the Guangxu era.
A Colophon to the Commentary on the *Buddhabhāṣita Gao-wang Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
Regarding the mantra for purifying the karma of speech:
"purify" means to wash away and completely eliminate it. When ordinary people create karma, it does not go beyond the two aspects of speech and action;
transgressions of speech are particularly easy to commit. One must thoroughly cleanse them before one can cultivate the Way and nourish one's nature.
"Xiūlì xiūlì xiūzhě" means "to cultivate and practice. "Lì" (benefit) refers to benefiting oneself while simultaneously benefiting others.
The two phrases are repeated for emphasis in order to clarify this point.
Mahāśrīmahā means "Great.
Because there is that which is greatly cultivated and maintained, one is subsequently able to benefit others.
Cultivation leads to benefit.
The more one cultivates it, the more proficient one becomes.
*Sarvasa* means "seeing. *Va* means "all things are equal. *Ha* means "all phenomena are causeless and quiescent."

Quiescence. It is the meaning of non-abiding purity and neither arising nor ceasing. It is said that the Buddha’s power shines universally, making no distinction between the noble and the humble, the wise and the ignorant, bringing all to the state of pure non-arising and non-ceasing.

The mantra for purifying the body encompasses the functions of seeing, hearing, and movement. To speak of "purifying the body" refers to the principle of "not looking at what is improper, not listening to what is improper, and not moving in what is improper.
To single out the two aspects of speech and action specifically refers to being circumspect in speech and prudent in conduct.
The path of cultivating the body has many aspects, *sūtrali sūtrali*. One must certainly cultivate it through various methods before it can be truly beneficial. *Sūmali*.
"Ma" is equivalent to "mahā. To say that one is able to cultivate it means that its benefit will necessarily be great;
this differs from the phrase "mahāśrī" (great auspiciousness) in terms of its depth and nuance. Svāhā.
*Sa* means the equality of all phenomena (*dharmas*). *Va* means the meaning of being beyond verbal expression. *Ha* means that all phenomena are without cause;

they are quiescent, non-abiding, and pure in the sense of neither arising nor ceasing. To say "the Buddha" is to speak of that which is beyond verbal expression, where there is no distinction between noble and base, or wise and foolish—all are brought to this purity of neither arising nor ceasing.
○ The Mantra for Pacifying the Earth:
Human beings tread upon the Great Earth and wear the Imperial Heaven upon their heads. If the Great Earth is at peace, the Imperial Heaven is likewise at peace.
One should therefore be careful in speech and prudent in conduct, so that in the end one may seek to stand before Heaven and Earth without shame. Thus, after purifying the body, one must—
Homage to the Earth Deity.
Homage to the Triple Jewel and all Buddhas.
In this world, twelve thousand years constitute one kalpa. Since the onset of chaos, there was nothing at all in the void.
Heaven opened at *zi* (the first hour). Earth was laid bare at *chou* (the second hour). Humanity was born at *yin* (the third hour).

As sentient beings and things gradually arose and increased until they were full, it is called the "Three Kalpas of Increase. When the cycles reached *you*, *xu*, and *hai* (the seventh, eighth, and ninth hours), sentient beings and things gradually became sparse and diminished;
thus, it is called the "Three Kalpas of Decrease. This is what is meant by *buddha-nāma*. *Bud* means "non-existence" (*mu*), and *dha* means "to carry" (*zai*). *Buddha-nāma* refers to—
The earth has nothing upon which to bear it. The Buddha’s cultivation of practice began three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* ago;

having cultivated until the attainment of *Maitreya* (Mudonam), he finally perfected the Great Way during the three *antarakalpas* of decrease. ○ Master Shiting said: "Śākyamuni’s cultivation of practice spanned three full *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
During the completion of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, he served Buddhas such as Ratnākara and others up to the Thousand Buddhas. During the second..."
For one full kalpa, he served Dīpaṃkara Buddha and continued through to a thousand Buddhas. During the third full kalpa, he made offerings to Vipaśyin Buddha and a thousand other Buddhas;
not a single one passed him by in vain. This coincided with the beginning of the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (the kalpa of decline).

At that time, the lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa was eighty-four thousand years, and their height was eight *zhang*. With the passing of every hundred years, their life span decreased by one [year].
Every year, the body decreases by one inch; after a thousand years have passed, the lifespan decreases by ten years and the body decreases by one foot.

In this manner, it continues to decrease until the lifespan is ten years and the body remains one foot tall—this is the end. During the kalpa of decrease (*apacaya-kalpa*), immeasurable beings are delivered.
The three preceding full kalpas are the three kalpas of increase (*vivarta-kalpa*). Every hundred years, the body increases by one inch and the lifespan increases by one year.

When one thousand years have passed, the body increases by one chi and the lifespan increases by ten years. In this manner, it increases until the lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years and the body reaches eight zhang.
Thus, three full cycles of increase and decrease constitute the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
only then does Śākyamuni declare that his myriad virtues are perfected.
Regarding "Oṃ Oṃ," there are two interpretations: one indicates that all spirits and deities are listening; the other indicates the meaning of the continuous flow of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Here, it should be understood as referring to the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing.
“Turu turu lu” refers collectively to those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, and transformations; it signifies that the Buddha universally delivers all beings.
*Ti-mi-sa-po-ho-ti*:

"Ti" refers to the furthest extremity of the earth. From the central lands to the regions of the barbarians and the Man-mo, extending to all places illuminated by the sun and moon and reached by frost and dew—all these are included.
*Sa-po-ho* has already been annotated in the preceding text; it signifies that the Buddha-dharma shines universally.
There is no distinction between east, west, south, or north, nor between the Central States and the barbarian tribes;
all are delivered to the state of purity, neither arising nor ceasing. The first two phrases encompass the words of a thousand ages, while this phrase points to the entire world.
This entire section collectively speaks of pervading both past and present and uniting the whole world: within this, the Buddha universally delivers all beings.
The *Buddhabhāṣita Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing* is one among many *Guanshiyin Sūtras*. It is called the *Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing* because this sūtra was transmitted from the kingdom of Gao-wang;
compared to various Tibetan scriptures, it is particularly reliable. As for the term "spoken by the Buddha" (*buddhabhāṣita*):
Because this sutra was personally bestowed by Avalokiteśvara, it is doubly precious compared to other sutras.
Regarding Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
"Avalokita" means to observe the causes and conditions of good and evil in the world; "Bodhi" means illumination; "Sattva" [means...]
This is called the "View of Words. It means to contemplate the causes and conditions of good and evil in the world and to perceive them clearly through illumination.
*Namo buddhāya*. *Namo dharmāya*. *Namo saṃghāya*.
*Namo* means taking refuge. In the Buddhist tradition, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute the Three Jewels.

The Buddha is the essence of nature (*xing*), which corresponds to the Confucian concept of "nature being what Heaven mandates. To take refuge in the Buddha (*namo fo*) is to clarify the mind and realize one's nature.

The Dharma is the path of cultivation, which corresponds to the Confucian concept of "following one's nature is called the Way. To take refuge in the Dharma (*namo fa*) is to practice and maintain [the teachings].
As for the realization of the mind and the seeing of nature, this is what is meant by the "Sangha" (the Great Assembly).

To take refuge in the Sangha means to instruct the great assembly in practice so that they may return to the mind and see their nature; this is precisely what is called the "Teaching" (Jiao) in the Confucian tradition of cultivating the Way.
There is a karmic affinity with the Buddha-land; the Buddhadharma arises through mutual causality.
This mutual causality is precisely what constitutes taking refuge. It is said that only those who possess a karmic affinity with the Buddha-land are able to take refuge in the Buddhadharma.
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity. These are the dharmas of the Buddha that have conditions. Regarding "permanence":

throughout one's entire life, it is as if it were a single day. Regarding "purity": one constantly practices the contemplation of purity; the two characters "lower purity" (*xià jìng*) and "light" (*guāng*) may be seen [in the text].
This refers to what is called "taking stillness as the primary principle to establish the ultimate standard for humanity. It need not be understood exclusively in terms of purity and quiescence.
Only those who are able to take stillness as their joy throughout their entire lives may be said to possess the karmic affinity for the Buddha-dharma.
Homage to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the great divine mantra. Homage to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā;
it is the unsurpassed mantra. Homage to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the unequaled mantra.
*Pāramitā* means "the other shore. The other shore is the stage of the Buddha’s enlightened mind and realization of one's nature (*xìng*).
*Praṇidhāna* (here rendered as *bōrě*) refers to possessing wisdom that skillfully destroys all afflictions and transforms them into sublime function.
*Mahā* means "great. There are six *pāramitās*: either generosity (*dāna*), or ethical discipline (*śīla*), or patience (*kṣānti*), or...
Vigor, meditative concentration, or wisdom each occupies one of the six perfections. Only prajñā (transcendent wisdom) can destroy all afflictions;
thus, it encompasses all six perfections and completes all myriad practices. At that very moment, one is endowed with the essence of Buddhahood.
This is what the Confucians mean when they say, "When I desire benevolence, benevolence arrives," and as the common proverb says:
"Cast down the butcher’s blade and you shall become a Buddha on the spot"—this is it. "Great Divinity" (*Mahādeva*) refers to its ultimate swiftness.
"Great Illumination" (*Mahāprabha*) refers to its ultimate brilliance. "Unsurpassed" (*Anuttara*) refers to the fact that nothing can be added to it.
"Peerless" (*Asamasama*) refers to the fact that there is nothing with which it may be matched. From the beginning up to this point constitutes one section. Stone.
Master Ting said: "That which is called the Great Divine Incantation is able to expel the demons of birth and death.

That which is called the Great Illuminating Incantation is able to shatter the darkness of ignorance throughout the long night. That which is called the Unsurpassed Incantation—Prajñā—is the supreme arousal of the bodhicitta."
This is the King of Dharmas; it is unsurpassed for this reason. This "Incomparable Mantra" is Prajñāpāramitā, the primary meaning of the six perfections; there is no Buddha who is its equal.
Homage to the Buddha Pure Light Secret and the Buddha Dharma-Treasury. Regarding "Pure Light":

the pure syllable at the crown of the head is explained as being below; that is, the *pāramitā*. Since it is pure and like the light of the sun, one should understand it as being interpreted by the syllable *śam* (quiescence).
"Secret" is explained in contrast to speech. As for the statement "taking refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma":
Without relying on verbal explanations, one causes the light of nature to remain eternally still; this alone is the True Dharma of the Buddha-treasury.
This is the Lion’s Roar, the Divine Footstep, the Profound King Buddha.
The Master had intercourse with a lion. When Śākyamuni was first born, he took seven steps by himself; with one hand he supported the heavens and with the other he pointed to the earth.
He opened his eyes and looked in the four directions, roaring like a lion to demonstrate that from the highest heaven to the lowest earth, I alone am supreme.
And through the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), one illuminates the dark and hidden realms. Master Shiting said:

"The Buddha attained the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and thereby perfected the Way. These six powers are: the power of the divine eye, the power of the divine ear, the power of knowing others' minds, the power of recollecting past lives, the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and the power of the divine feet—which is the power of mastery over will (*kāmadhenu-ṛddhi*). As for the power of the divine feet: in a single *kṣaṇa*..."
And he arrived at the four continents. As for King You (Yin), he dwells in stillness and silence, unmoving.
The Buddha addressed the Buddhas Sumerupradīpa and Dharmarakṣa.
As recorded in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Tathāgata told Subhūti: "In the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained nothing regarding the Teacher’s Dharma.

This is because the Buddha-Dharma must be such that the mind dwells nowhere; thus, by telling Subhūti that there is nothing to be attained regarding the Dharma, he was precisely upholding and protecting the Buddha-Dharma.

The Vajragarbha, Siṃhavikrīḍita, Buddhavara, and Ṛddhivikrīḍita Buddhas—those recorded by Vajragarbha—possess both material forms and empty forms. The adorned dharmic images they manifest are wondrous and supernatural, all like a lion sporting in the world.
Because of this, people of the world regard these as the supreme excellence of the Buddhas.
One regards this realm as precious; in reality, it is nothing more than the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
As for the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha:

"Medicine" (yào) takes healing illness as its function, while "Master" (shī) takes instruction and guidance as his capacity. Regarding "Lapis Lazuli" (liúlí), it borrows from the name of the sovereign of the Buddha-land.

The blue gemstone, being exceedingly clear and pure, serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s body; it signifies that in healing sentient beings, one must first address the nature and substance of their being, which is supremely luminous.
The Buddha Samantaprabhāsa-guṇa-parvatarāja dwells within a mountain,
yet his merits pervade the ten directions; this is equivalent to the Confucian ideal of "light shining upon the four quarters and reaching to the heights above and depths below."
The Buddha Ratnarāja-suvyavasthita-kuśala-karman dwells in one direction, having performed virtuous deeds.
These are the seven Buddhas of the past.
Master Shiting said: 1. In Sanskrit, Vipaśyin Buddha; in Chinese, "Perfected Wisdom-Light. 2. In Sanskrit, Śikhin Buddha;
in Chinese, "Great Wisdom-Light," which is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). 3. In Sanskrit, Viśvabhū Buddha;
in Chinese, "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. 4. In Sanskrit, Krakucchanda Buddha; in Chinese, [omitted].
He has eternally severed all afflictions. In the fivefold Sanskrit language, he is called Kanakamuni Buddha;
in Chinese, he is called Nengren Jimo (The Benevolent One Who is Silent). Because he is silent, he does not abide in saṃsāra; because he is benevolent, he does not abide in nirvāṇa.
With compassion and wisdom operating in tandem, his benefit to sentient beings is inexhaustible. All those mentioned above refer to those who have already perfected their cultivation and practice.
Regarding the names of the thousand Buddhas of the future Bhadrakalpa, according to the *Record of the Thirty Buddha-lands*, these thousand children were born in the country upstream of the Ganges.
Their mother gave birth to a mass of flesh, which she cast into the Ganges; it was then collected by the king of another kingdom.
He was raised and later grew up to be extremely brave and robust. Wherever he went on military expeditions, there were none whom he did not defeat and subdue.
Next, he marched against his own country of birth. The king was deeply distressed. His mother, the queen, ascended the high tower on the eastern side of the city and said to him, "You are my son;
why do you commit such an act that violates the natural order? At first he did not believe her, but when she explained the matter in detail, he let go of his bow.
He prostrated himself before his mother and then bowed to his father. Confucian scholars of the world maintain that the Buddha is without father and without sovereign;
therefore, they do not record the origins or whereabouts of other Buddhas. This [text], however, alone records them.
The names of the one thousand five hundred Buddhas, the ten thousand five hundred Buddhas, the five hundred transformation Buddhas,

and the ten billion Vajragarbha Buddhas are the names of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. As for those listed below that extend into the future, they are all spoken by way of metaphor regarding those who will practice and uphold [the teachings] in the future.

Dīpaṃkara Buddha is none other than the Tathāgata Samantaraśmirāja. The reason this text mentions Dīpaṃkara alone is that it emphasizes that one must first attain concentration (*samādhi*) before one can achieve tranquility (*śamatha*).
Regardless of whether one considers the past or the future, those who seek tranquility must first seek concentration. This applies throughout the entire scroll.

The invocation of the Buddhas' names all possesses profound principles; how could they be cited in a mere superficial or miscellaneous manner? From "The Buddha Pure Light Secret" up to this point constitutes one section:
the names of the six Buddhas of the six directions.
This phrase refers to the six directions—east, south, west, north, above, and below—mentioned in the subsequent text. It collectively encompasses the human life cycle:

born in the east, growing in the south, maturing in the west, returning in the north, the *hun* spirit ascending to heaven, and the *po* spirit descending to earth; hence, they are called the "six directions."
In the east is the Buddha King of the Sublime Sound of the Moon in the Palace of Jewel Light.
"Jewel Light" refers to the preciousness of the essential nature of speech. "Palace of the Moon" refers to the moon's sprout; "sound" refers to its reflection.
This signifies that the light of the essential nature of a person at birth is like a reflection within the moon; its substance is exceedingly subtle, yet it is real.
It is most supreme and most wondrous.
As for the Buddha King of Tree-Root Flowers in the south,
he says that "having roots" means that [the tree] can produce flowers of its own accord.
In the western direction is the King of Soaps, the Buddha Śakti-jvālā-kusuma-rāja.
This world is like a great dyeing ground; only one whose supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are vast can remain unstained by the fires of the world.
In the north is the Buddha Pure Moon Palace;
after a person's life has ended, they return to purity, like the moon at the end of its waning phase.
Above is the Buddha Infinite Vigor Jewel Head.

The "Origin" (Yuán) is the Primordial Beginning. When the pure and clear qi ascends, one is naturally able to cultivate diligent progress without ceasing, thereby preserving that original goodness of the primordial source.
This refers to the Buddha Benevolent Tranquility Moon-Sound King (Shàn-jì-yuè-yīn-wáng Fó) below.
The turbid energies descend like shadows within the moon, all returning to quiescent extinction.
The immeasurable Buddhas—
all these Buddhas— are accomplished through cultivation over immeasurable kalpas.
Prabhūtaratna Buddha:
his nature and essence are such that they are worthy of being treasured. Śākyamuni Buddha.

The meaning of Śākya is "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren). The meaning of Muni is "Silent Stillness" (Jimo). "Capable Benevolent One" refers to the boundless nature of the mind, which encompasses all things.
"Silent Stillness" refers to the fundamental quiescence of the essential nature, wherein movement and stillness do not interfere with one another.
Maitreya Buddha:
"Mi" means there is nothing that does not reach upward; it refers to the nature and essence reaching upward without exception. "Le" means to restrain it, so as not to allow it to reach downward.
"Akṣobhya" (A-ge-chu):
"Chu" (閦) means the beginning. "A" (阿) signifies the very commencement of human existence. ○ Master Shiting said:
"Akṣobhya is the unmoving, eternally abiding *dharmatā*; thus, it carries this same meaning."
Amitābha Buddha is the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. The six phrases—east, south, west, north, above, and below—state that every person possesses the Buddha-nature.
The subsequent lines state that through the power of cultivation and practice, one thereby becomes the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. (6)
The title [of this section] now concludes the six directions. Furthermore, it forms a separate segment:
"All sentient beings in the center, within the Buddha-world.
Here, "sentient beings" refers to both humans and other creatures. From the beginning of creation until the present, there have always been Buddhas sustaining the world; therefore, it is so stated.
Within the Buddha-worlds,
whether walking or staying upon the earth or in the midst of space, he regards all sentient beings with compassion,
causing each to find peace and rest.
It is said that through meditative concentration one attains stillness; only then can one bring peace to people and peace to all things.
Practice this day and night, and let your mind constantly seek to recite this sutra. It can extinguish the suffering of birth and death and subdue all poisonous harms.
"Subduing" (*fu*) refers to what is called "subduing the mind" in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. "Poisonous harm" (*dúhài*) refers precisely to various deluded and evil thoughts.

The Buddha spoke these words because he granted that those who seek fame and achievement would obtain fame and achievement, those who seek wealth and status would obtain wealth and status, and those who seek offspring would obtain offspring.
Yet, as for these "poisonous words" regarding the poisonous harm of birth and death, it was likely because he feared people would enter [the path of] the sons [of the Buddha].
Greed, anger, and delusion alone.
Namo (Namo and Namu are interchangeable) to the Greatly Radiant Avalokiteśvara, the Illuminating Radiance Avalokiteśvara, and the Sublime Radiance Avalokiteśvara.
He revealed to Avalokiteśvara and Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva:
"The elder previously called Starlight (Jyotirasa) held medicinal herbs and bestowed them universally upon sentient beings;
there were none of the four hundred and four illnesses that were not cured, and he was thus able to extinguish the suffering of birth and death."

The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, younger brother of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed the Elder Vidyutprabha, saying: "My elder brother merely treats the diseases of the body, yet does not heal the disease of the mind.
He takes medicine in both hands and bestows it upon sentient beings, whereby the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion are all extinguished."
The wisdom of bodhi is immediately born; the ten unwholesome deeds are transformed into the ten wholesome deeds; the six sense-objects are transformed into the six perfections;
and attachment to existence is transformed into non-abiding. This is what is meant by "subduing and eliminating poisonous harms."

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: Mañjuśrī’s literary brilliance is far superior to that of worldly scholars; his virtue and wisdom are sufficient to serve as a teacher for humanity, and he is one who brings benefit and salvation.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Virtue that is all-pervading is called "Universal" (Pǔ). One who protects those above and benefits those below is called "Worthy" (Xián).
The Bodhisattvas Ākāśagarbha and Kṣitigarbha refer to those [who act] throughout the heavens above and the earth below.
"One ten-thousand bodhisattvas on the Cool Mountain Jewel" (Qīngliáng Bǎoshān yīwàn púsà).
"Jewel Mountain" refers to the square inch [of the heart]. It means that when this mind is cool and clear, one is able to clearly perceive all things and all thoughts.
Some say the Cool Mountain Jewel is the abode of Kṣitigarbha Rāja, who currently resides in Jinling; here, it refers to the mind.
He said: "I fear this may not be so. I do not know whether the 'spiritual terrace' (lingtai) or 'square-inch spiritual terrace' mentioned earlier refers to the Buddha’s spiritual terrace.
It is borrowed merely as a metaphor for the mind's cool clarity; why must Mount Baoshan be viewed as a literal reality?"
The Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa-rāja transformed the Bodhisattva Jinaśreṣṭha.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata," it refers to the original nature of a person; this is what Confucianism calls "returning to the beginning.

To say that one does not lose their original nature means that their radiance universally illumines all things, such that even though external conditions undergo a thousand transformations and myriad changes, they are naturally able to [remain as they are].
He surpassed him. ○ Master Shiting said: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
As for 'Universal Radiance' (Puguang), its light shines everywhere, leaving not even the slightest thing to escape it."
Recite this sutra in every thought-moment.
"In every thought-moment" means that not a single thought is interspersed with anything else.
Then the Seven World-Honored Buddhas spoke the mantra, saying:

The "Seven Buddhas" refers to the seven past Buddhas. "Dhāraṇī" (zhòu) means to invoke or bless; it is by means of this Dharma that one invokes them, so as to cause [the practitioner] to follow their prayers.
A dhāraṇī may be the secret speech of the various Buddhas, arising from the wondrous application of their mental faculties and the power of their hidden grace.
It is inconceivable and beyond the reach of thought. It may also be the name of a lord of ghosts and spirits; by calling upon this lord, demons and malevolent spirits flee and hide.
"Līlavīlāpati" means to depart from all the winds and waves of the world.
*Ko ha ko ha ti ha ca*:
All phenomena are without cause; they are quiescent and non-abiding. This is the meaning of purity, being neither born nor extinguished.
*Dhāraṇītejaprabha-saṃgraha*:
It subdues the heterodox and establishes the orthodox; it eradicates evil and gives rise to good—all these are comprehensively upheld. *Nihārade*.
This means to sweep away all that is deviant, false, good, and evil.
*Vīrya-nirdeśa* (or *Vīrya-vini*) refers to the unremitting diligence among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Mahākātyāyana: "Kātya" refers to your person; "Mahākātya" signifies the vastness of your person.
You are the True Spirit and Sovereign Lord.
The spirit of true nature accords with the virtue of Heaven; it is the manifestation of the Supreme Heaven—without sound and without smell.
*Svāhā*: *Sva* means the sense of being beyond verbal expression; *ha* means that all phenomena (*dharma*) are equal; *hā* means that all phenomena are without [intrinsic nature].

The cause is the meaning of quiescence, non-abiding, purity, and neither arising nor ceasing. It is said that because the Buddha is beyond verbal expression, all things throughout the ten thousand ages are brought to the state of purity, neither arising nor ceasing.
Annotated Commentary on the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra of Gao Wang Guanshiyin* (End).
The Original Origin of the *Gao Wang Jing*:
In the past, during the Five Dynasties period, there was a King named Gao Huan who served as the Prefect of Xiangzhou. He was fond of killing. Once, while visiting Baozang...
The official Sun Jingde had mistakenly committed a grave offense and was imprisoned, facing execution.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a monk who said, "If you recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one thousand times, you shall be released from this legal penalty. Jingde replied, "I am currently in prison;
how can I obtain the scriptures? The monk said, "I will orally transmit them to you. Upon waking, Jingde wrote them down and did not forget anything.

With a devout mind, he recited [the scripture] until he had completed nine hundred repetitions. The official documents were finalized, and the King consequently ordered him to the marketplace for execution.
Jingde asked the supervising officer about the distance to the market. The officer asked, "For what reason do you ask?
Jingde replied, "Last night in a dream, a monk commanded me to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one thousand times, saying that I would thereby escape death. Now..."

"One hundred is still lacking; I request that you proceed slowly along the road so that I may urgently complete the count. When he reached the marketplace, the supervising official proclaimed the imperial decree and struck him down.
Yet his body and head remained unharmed, and the blade broke into three pieces. When presented to the King, the King was startled and questioned him:
"What sorcery do you possess to allow this? Jingde replied, "In truth, I have no sorcery. It is because I was in prison and feared death."
He prayed to Avalokiteśvara. Suddenly, in a dream, a monk instructed him to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one thousand times, saying that such was the merit to be obtained.
The King said to Jingde, "You are superior to me; how are you any different from a Buddha?

The King summoned the jailer and ordered him to write out this sūtra. He then commanded that each of the prisoners condemned to death should recite it one thousand times before being executed. [He] took...
The responses were entirely verified. The King then issued an edict ordering the people to recite it universally in order to attest to the fruits of merit.
Consequently, it became widely known in the world as the *Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing*.
